# System Design in Go: Capstone Track

These are **design-and-build labs**: each specifies a small system, implementation boundaries, failure cases, and acceptance evidence. They extend the book's runnable beginner projects. Code fragments illustrate core boundaries; they are not complete deployable services.

The topic selection comes from the two contents-page photos in [Harshit Khosla's Go project post](https://x.com/Harry_The_Nerd/status/2121189400965173476). The explanations and exercises here are original Go implementations and design work, rather than summaries of the photographed books or claims about commercial systems' internal architectures.

## Prerequisites and working method

Use Go modules, HTTP handlers, contexts, goroutines, SQL transactions, and table-driven tests from earlier parts of this book. Begin with [requirements, estimates, and scaling](../../18-distributed-infra/150a-system-design-method-and-capacity.qmd), then choose one project. Use local fixtures, fake providers, and synthetic records; an external account is not required.

Keep each exercise in its own module. Record the actual Go and dependency versions in the module files. A useful layout is `cmd/server`, `internal/domain`, `internal/store`, and `internal/adapters`, plus migrations and deterministic fixtures. Start with one complete request path; avoid creating empty abstractions for every possible service.

For every lab deliver an API contract, data schema, runnable vertical slice, capacity estimate, failure test, and short design record. Mark which state is authoritative, which state can be rebuilt, and when an acknowledgment becomes durable. Run `go test ./...` and `go test -race ./...` for your implementation, then measure one overload or recovery scenario.

## Suggested progression

Start with the existing shortener, KV store, and chat builds. Then complete hashing, IDs, and the queue lab. For fan-out, work through notifications, feeds, and autocomplete. For large bytes, build object storage before video and file sync. For geospatial work, proceed from proximity to nearby friends to routes. Finish with reservations, payments, the wallet, and the matching engine, where transactional state and deterministic recovery are central.

Metrics and alerting apply throughout. Record throughput, p99 latency, oldest pending age, and memory under failure rather than treating a diagram as proof that a system scales. When a prototype loses data or duplicates an external effect, describe the precise boundary and the next mechanism needed to change that guarantee.
